extracted.intended_audience: general readers who want to develop a sense of humor and be funnier in social or performance settings
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, general-audience guidance for developing a sense of humor, writing/delivering jokes and one-liners, and using different comedic techniques in everyday and performance contexts. Covers skill-building, ethics (punching up/down), timing, types of humor, and sources of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure out what makes you laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to what genuinely makes you laugh rather than forcing laughter; understand that laughter often comes more easily around others and from benign violations (surprising but not serious norm violations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't force a laugh — forced laughter is obvious. Note personal triggers and contexts that make you laugh, and use that to develop authentic humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to what other people find funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe what friends and family laugh at and study comedians, funny movies, sitcoms, improv shows, and comedy podcasts to learn different styles and what elicits laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People-watching helps you learn how humor functions for different audiences; what makes others laugh may not suit you, but seeing reactions helps you understand timing, subject matter, and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hang around and learn from funny people
rubrics_metrics.description: Surround yourself with funny people—professional comedians or funny friends—and note what they do and how they do it to build a toolbox of techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immerse yourself but also participate; take notes on admired traits and adapt techniques to your own voice rather than simply copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make an effort to laugh and smile more
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase laughing and smiling in daily life to develop a habit and make humor more natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include setting a timer to fake-laugh or smile for a minute until it becomes real; looking for humor in mundane misfortunes and prioritizing laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have fun, be yourself, and trust your sense of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity is key—being yourself helps you feel relaxed and confident, which makes it easier to be funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't try to make every comment a joke; stay present and react to the moment. Your unique perspective is your comedic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorize a few simple jokes and one-liners
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and keep a small stock of clean, simple jokes and one-liners to use socially when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose jokes that fit your style, are harmless and not cliché. Practice delivery and timing; memes and witty comments can also serve as shareable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the element of surprise (misdirection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create humor by setting up expectations and then subverting them so the audience is surprised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misdirection works like a magic trick—direct attention and then reveal an unexpected punchline. Examples include classic two-meaning jokes and clever one-liners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic timing: strike while the iron is hot
rubrics_metrics.description: Good humor depends on pacing, delivery, rhythm, and pauses; deliver jokes at the right moment to maximize impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to the conversation and when a one-liner or comeback will land; avoid delayed comebacks (thinking of them hours later). Use pauses deliberately (e.g., 'Take my wife…please').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Rule of 3 (comedic triple)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure jokes with three parts—set expectations, build anticipation, and deliver a surprising third element as the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three-part structure heightens humor by creating a pattern and then breaking it. Example: Jon Stewart Thanksgiving joke demonstrating setup, build, and shocking punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch up (target those with more power), avoid punching down
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct jokes toward people or institutions with more power rather than marginalized or less powerful individuals to avoid cruelty and bullying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punching up can 'speak truth to power'; punching sideways (self-deprecation) is acceptable. Avoid punching down because it can harm people and backfire socially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience and be careful not to offend
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the room and tailor humor to the group's mood, interests, and sensitivities to avoid causing offense or being inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If people are serious, keep humor low-key; use accessible subjects that most people relate to; avoid jokes at funerals, religious events, or other highly sensitive contexts. Misplaced humor can be seen as harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice making jokes and funny comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Like any skill, comedy improves with repetition: practice delivery, timing, and writing jokes, starting with trusted friends and expanding to strangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for constructive feedback, develop a 'tough skin' for misses, and expect that even great comedians sometimes fail with an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to appreciate witty wordplay and puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use linguistic play—puns and wordplay—that exploits multiple meanings or similar sounds to create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordplay can arise from accidental slips or intentional cleverness; practice switching meanings or sounds (examples provided) and consider audience tolerance for puns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Create humor through a gap between expectations and reality—saying or presenting something that contrasts with what is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony can be verbal (jokes) or situational (film examples); craft setups that lead the audience one way and flip them to reveal ironic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try observational humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Find comedy in everyday life by pointing out the absurdities and unnoticed details of ordinary situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be observant and translate relatable minutiae into jokes; observational humor often resonates widely because it points to shared experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden your horizons to get more material
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquire knowledge across varied subjects so you can craft jokes that connect with different audiences and make surprising parallels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Range of knowledge increases relatable topics and clever juxtapositions (e.g., connecting theoretical physics and pop culture) and signals intelligence in humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and study the subject of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Study joke books, memoirs, and works by comedians; analyze why certain jokes succeed or fail to internalize comedic principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended authors and memoirs (e.g., Tina Fey, Steve Martin) provide examples; dissect jokes structurally and thematically to learn craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be an active listener to collect material and time jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Listen attentively to others to understand feelings and notice opportunities for empathetic, relevant humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain eye contact, avoid planning your next line, and pause to think—active listening helps you craft better, more believable humor tailored to the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use callbacks to amplify laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer back to a previous joke later in the set or conversation to often get an equal or bigger laugh the second time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many comedians use callbacks strategically; ensure the callback is recognizable and enhances the running joke rather than confusing the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't laugh at your own jokes until others do
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid laughing at your own joke prematurely, which can signal trying too hard and spoil the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold composure until the audience responds; laughing at yourself too early can undercut effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sure your jokes are unique to you; don't copy others' style
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a personal comedic voice and avoid imitating other comedians' material or style verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use known jokes, pick genuinely funny, harmless ones and adapt them to your persona to avoid clichés and accusations of theft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure jokes are appropriate and not insulting
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose topics that fit the context and avoid insulting or targeting people's appearance, religion, or other sensitive attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the environment before telling a joke; humor that insults or singles people out can harm relationships and is not funny to many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid picking on any one person too much
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't repeatedly make someone the butt of jokes; over-targeting can hurt feelings and cease to be funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit how often you single someone out and monitor reactions; stop if someone seems offended or uncomfortable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful making jokes about religion and politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitive topics like religion and politics can be comedic but carry high risk of offense if you 'go too far.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tread carefully, assess audience leanings, and avoid escalation; consider avoiding these subjects in mixed or unknown company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of humor for wellbeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and laughter provide physical, cognitive, emotional, and social benefits—reduced stress, improved mood and creativity, stronger relationships, decreased pain, boosted immunity, and relaxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humor as a tool for mental and physical health; intentionally seek laugh-inducing activities to gain these benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use laughter to cope with stress and anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can lighten heavy subjects and help release tension, anger, and anxiety when used appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice what makes you defensive and find humor to defuse it; humor can help with anxiety but should be used sensitively around others' distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take yourself less seriously and mine embarrassing moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use your own embarrassing or cringe-worthy experiences as material to appear spontaneous and relatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-deprecating stories can build rapport and reduce fear of judgment; they also help you be more spontaneous and forgiving of mistakes.
